questions.question: Q: What is the 'prosumer' and how has digital media created this role?
questions.correctAnswer: A prosumer is someone who both produces and consumes media content. Digital media — smartphones, social media platforms, editing apps — has enabled audiences to create and share content, not just passively consume it. Examples include YouTube vloggers, TikTok creators, and fan fiction writers.

questions.question: Q: How do algorithms affect what audiences see on social media?
questions.correctAnswer: Algorithms analyse user behaviour (likes, shares, watch time) to personalise content feeds. They prioritise content likely to generate engagement, creating filter bubbles where users see posts that reinforce their existing views. This can polarise opinions and limit exposure to diverse perspectives.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate the impact of social media on democratic participation.
questions.correctAnswer: Social media enables direct political engagement, rapid mobilisation (Arab Spring, BLM), and gives voice to marginalised groups. However, filter bubbles polarise debate, misinformation spreads faster than truth, and algorithmic amplification rewards extreme content. The net effect depends on regulation, media literacy, and platform design.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the impact of social media on media audiences and industries. [15 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Social media has fundamentally transformed the relationship between media audiences and industries, creating both opportunities and challenges. For audiences, social media has empowered participation. Prosumers create and share content, challenging the traditional producer-audience hierarchy. Jenkins' participatory culture shows fans as active creators, not passive consumers. Audiences can engage directly with producers, access diverse content, and build communities around shared interests. However, algorithms shape what audiences see. Filter bubbles created by personalisation can narrow perspectives and polarise debate. The attention economy rewards engaging content over accurate content, enabling misinformation. The viral spread of content prioritises emotional impact over truth. For industries, social media has created new business models. Influencer marketing has become a major revenue stream. Brands can target audiences with unprecedented precision using data analytics. Streaming services use social media for distribution and promotion. But industries have also lost control. Audiences can publicly criticise brands, negative content can go viral, and the speed of social media means crises escalate rapidly. Traditional gatekeepers (newspapers, broadcasters) have less power to set the agenda. Regulation struggles to keep pace.
